latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Insufficient circulating glucocorticoid effect during physiologic stress. This removes permissive cortisol support for vascular catecholamine response, hepatic gluconeogenesis, free-water clearance, and inflammatory stress tolerance.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Mineralocorticoid deficiency and renal salt wasting
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Insufficient aldosterone effect reduces distal sodium reabsorption and potassium/hydrogen secretion. It is strongest when the adrenal cortex itself is unable to produce mineralocorticoid; it may be minimal when the axis problem is central.

Acute illness, surgery, trauma, fever, vomiting, or missed replacement creates a demand spike that exceeds available cortisol reserve. This is the dynamic trigger that converts compensated adrenal insufficiency into crisis.
Cortisol deficiency reduces vascular alpha-adrenergic tone and makes hypotension poorly responsive to fluids and catecholamines until glucocorticoid is replaced.
Renal sodium wasting, vomiting, diarrhea, reduced intake, and impaired vascular tone converge on intravascular depletion and prerenal azotemia.
Cortisol deficiency increases vasopressin tone and impairs free-water excretion; mineralocorticoid deficiency and sodium loss further deepen hyponatremia.
Aldosterone deficiency and renal hypoperfusion reduce potassium and hydrogen ion excretion, producing hyperkalemia, non-anion or mixed acidosis, ECG changes, paralysis, and arrhythmia risk.

Cortisol deficiency reduces hepatic gluconeogenesis and fasting stress tolerance. Children, older adults, low glycogen reserve, and concomitant insulin therapy are especially vulnerable to hypoglycemia.
Cortisol deficiency and precipitating illness drive nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, anorexia, and diarrhea. These symptoms also prevent oral steroid intake and amplify volume depletion.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Accumulated injury from delayed steroid replacement
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Hours to days without parenteral glucocorticoid allow shock, hypoglycemia, hyperkalemia, hyponatremic encephalopathy, AKI, and cardiac arrest hazards to accumulate.

supportive_care: Draw cortisol and ACTH before hydrocortisone if immediately feasible, but do not delay parenteral steroid treatment for testing.
Frequent vital-sign reassessment with MAP, heart rate, temperature, mental status, urine output, and orthostatic symptoms when stable enough.
Serial electrolytes and glucose every few hours early: sodium, potassium, bicarbonate, creatinine, BUN, and bedside glucose.
Continuous ECG monitoring when potassium is elevated or ECG changes are present.
Use isotonic saline for hypovolemia; add dextrose-containing fluids when hypoglycemia, low glycogen reserve, or insulin-treated diabetes context is present.
Avoid overly rapid correction of severe chronic hyponatremia; track sodium trajectory and neurologic status.
Treat precipitating infection, gastroenteritis, surgical stress, trauma, or medication cause in parallel with endocrine rescue.
Transition from parenteral stress dosing to oral physiologic replacement only after hemodynamic stability, oral intake, and electrolyte improvement.
Assess need for mineralocorticoid replacement after hydrocortisone stress dose is reduced, especially when hyperkalemia, salt wasting, or high renin persists.
Provide sick-day rules, emergency injectable hydrocortisone, medical alert identification, and clear return precautions before discharge.
In patients with diabetes, proactively adjust insulin and monitor for steroid-induced hyperglycemia while avoiding hypoglycemia recurrence.
In suspected autoimmune polyendocrine context, screen thyroid and diabetes status, but ensure glucocorticoid coverage before intensifying thyroid hormone.
